Data: [TidyTuesday 2026-09-01](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2026/2026-09-01).

The week's data labels 5,793 landmarks with one of four words: castle, fortress, palace or ruin.
The words look like four kinds of building.
They are closer to two kinds, five hundred years apart.

A medieval castle is one building doing two jobs.
It is where a lord lives and it is what keeps the lord alive.
The half-century from 1300 is the height of that arrangement: 238 castles and ruins founded against 24 fortresses and palaces.
Then the two jobs come apart.
An artillery fort has no hall, and a palace has no wall worth the name.
Up to 1650, fortresses and palaces are 46% of new foundings.
From 1650 on they never fall below 75% again, and the fortified home never returns.

The figure is drawn as the thing it counts.
Each half-century is one merlon of a wall, and the gap either side is what makes the top edge a crenellation rather than a row of columns.
The waterline is zero.
Above it stands the fortified home, whether it is still standing or has fallen to a ruin.
Below it, in the reflection, are the two buildings that replaced it.

Three cautions, and the first is the largest.
Only 3,610 of the 5,793 landmarks carry a founding year, and the gap is not evenly spread: 77% of palaces are dated against 56% of castles.
A later building is easier to date, so the lower wall is flattered by the same records that thin the upper one.
The shape survives that bias, because the collapse after 1600 is visible in the castle count on its own, but the wall is a shape and not a census.

Second, a ruin is a state and not a purpose.
Most ruins here are medieval castles, and the median ruin is founded in 1300 against 1350 for the median standing castle, which is why they are counted together above the waterline.
That is the figure's choice, not the data's.

Third, this is a Wikidata census before it is an architectural one.
France, Italy and Germany hold about 350 landmarks each and Japan 297, which says as much about who writes Wikipedia articles as about who built castles.
